subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, April 18, consideration of the motion of the Minister of Finance that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself again into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the third time
that the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) has brought down his budget and also the third time that I have had the honour to rise on this side of the house and offer the views of those who sit around me in connection with the matters which he proposes. I again congratulate him, as I have done on previous occasions, on the clearness of the presentation which he has made, and on the moderation of the tone which he has adopted and of the language which has been used in presenting the annual statement of this great dominion. He knows and hon. members generally know that my congratulations cannot go very much further than that in view of the fact that those who sit around me and I myself feel that this budget is born of policies which are diametrically opposed to those which we endorse and which we believe to be for the benefit of Canada. It may be made clear before I get through that I am not particularly enamoured of the budget which my hon. friend has brought down. I do, however, want him to feel-and while it is a commonplace, at the same time even a sincere commonplace may be worth while expressing-this is a criticism not of the Minister of Finance as such or personally, but of those policies to which I have referred.
I could have wished, as a matter of fact, that for his sake the day for bringing down this budget had been a little longer delayed in order that the country might have got out of its mind the British budget which was brought down just the day before he addressed the house. That was a budget wherein the people of Great Britain, a country which has borne the load since the early twenties, were able to show a surplus of

something like $150,000,000 at a time when customs duties were imposed, not gallows high as they are here, but having regard to revenue as well as to industry. That budget was in marked contrast to that which my hon. friend presented and which, when all was said and done, instead of showing a surplus, showed a deficit of something like $24,000,000 on ordinary account. May I say also that my hon. friend's budget showed a mistake predicting customs duties notwithstanding that year after year he has been modestly lowering his estimate in the hope some day to overtake the drop. It showed a mistake in prediction of customs duties of something like $6,000,000; last year he predicted that he would receive at least $72,000,000 in customs duties and he received something like $65,900,000. The year before he had predicted $80,000,000 and he fell below that by $8,000,000. I repeat, that perhaps he was not too fortunate in having to present his budget as he did the day after the British one.
In a phrase his budget, it seems to me, shows that the government are systematically living on the future of this country and the future that they are hoping for fails to arrive. I realize that a budget does not have the piquancy of a best seller and that generally there is nothing of dramatic interest to be found in a budget speech, but as a rule, having regard to the changes in the times, one would have thought my hon. friend, in the long speech which he delivered, would have been able to produce at least some item of liveliness outside the gold tax to which I will refer in a moment. I could not help feeling that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) had evidently not had very much to do with the preparation of this budget, because it did not satisfy the longing of his soul which he expressed in the house the other night when he intimated that the people were clamouring for something new and that governments had been slow to depart from the beaten track. He said, to quote his words in full:
In this country, as in other countries, people have been staggering along under conditions that have been difficult, and have been clamouring for something out of the ordinary. Peoples all over the world have been very restive with governments because governments have been slow to depart from the beaten track.
I read this budget with the thought: Is there not some place here where the Minister of Finance has departed from the beaten track, if for nothing other than to satisfy the ambitions and longings of the Minister of Trade and Commerce? But I

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
find that even silver, which is a favourite subject of my hon. friend, is not mentioned in the budget. That would have been a step aside from the beaten track for him.
Even the turnover tax, which has been mentioned in years gone by, is not to be found in this budget. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), speaking in the house in 1928, at a time when he had not the responsibilities of office, was most urgent that a turnover tax should be imposed in this country. Here was an opportunity for the Minister of Finance to step aside from the beaten track to give the people, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce says, something they are clamouring for and to impose some new form of taxation. The statement made by the Prime Minister in 1928 in Hansard at page1 1252 was:
May I remind the house that last year 1 argued that, in my judgment, the fairest method of taxation in the world was to be found in the turnover tax. I have not changed my mind in that regard; I think there should be a turnover tax collected every month.
A little further on he said, with characteristic modesty:
I pointed out when discussing this question last year that the idea was not original with myself. I do not claim originality for it; it has been submitted to the house before and is endorsed by sound economists and financiers. I urge the Minister of Finance, therefore, to take it into his serious consideration.
That turnover tax is not found in this budget. The Prime Minister in 1931 again advocated it and again indicated his disappointment that it had not been put upon the statute book. He said-I am quoting from Hansard of 1931, at page 3307:
I should like to have seen applied in Canada some new system of taxation, and he is quite right when he says it is not at all probable that I shall ever have a chance to try a new form of taxation, because it is not at all likely that I shall ever again submit ways and means to this house. I am not without hope, however, that some Minister of Finance reviewing the means by which taxes may be raised will realize the values and benefits accruing from a turnover tax. . . .
Sir, it has not been my privilege to introduce any new forms of taxation to this country at this time. ... I do not for a single moment disguise the fact that I would like to have done so. I should like to have written a budget which would have expressed my views with respect to taxation in Canada. That privilege has not been given, and it never will be.
I only want to say to the Prime Minister, who I am sorry is not in his seat, being indisposed I understand, that he ought not to feel too badly about it. He is tender-hearted and if he did bring down a system of taxation of this kind he would be sure to change it before the budget was through. He ought to leave
it to the flinty Minister of Finance to impose taxation.
But if my right hon. friend the Prime Minister is looking for the privilege of having it said of him that he imposed taxation in this country surely his ambition is satisfied in the increase of the sales tax from one to six per cent, in the imposition of an excise tax which did not exist when he came into power but which has been put up to three per cent, in the imposition of a two cent tax on sugar, in taking away exemptions from the sales tax, in the reduction of exemptions in the income tax; in these and in every other field of taxation I think my hon. friends opposite will be given full marks and will be held fully responsible when they come to the people of Canada, for having invented and imposed many new and onerous forms of taxation. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister need not have any regrets, I think. The Minister of Finance has enjoyed and exercised to the full the privilege, as the Prime Minister calls it, of levying and imposing taxation, as the people of this country have good reason to know.
But there might be some other method whereby the beaten track could be avoided and something new put into this budget. I have mentioned this before but in view of the fact that the other night the Prime Minister in the House of Commons dealt with debt conversion, let me remind this house that it was not so long ago that the Prime Minister had a very distinct and definite plan for retiring the national debt by means of a sinking fund which was to be established and a certain amount set aside each year. I quote from Hansard of 1928, page 1249:
Mr. Bennett: The finance minister said that the only way to pay off the debt was out of surplus. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there is another way in which we can pay off our national debt, and that is to pass a statute by which we provide that a given sum per annum shall be set aside to pay off the national debt of Canada.
That was in 1928. Of course, Mr. Speaker, you cannot pay off national debts and set up sinking funds unless you have surpluses, and you do not have surpluses with Tory governments in power. So it is all right for my hon. friend the Prime Minister to advocate the setting up of a sinking fund when Liberals are in power and piling up surpluses, but we hear nothing about that plan to-day when deficits are the order of the hour.
Another way in which my hon. friend could have got out of the beaten track and satisfied the Minister of Trade and Commerce was to have abolished the sales tax. That was an "iniquitous" tax according to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) in 1928. That was a
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

tax which the Prime Minister in Hansard of 1927 at page 397 called the "poor man's income tax." That is the tax which was referred to by the Minister of Justice in Hansard of 1928 at page 1124, when he pictured the poor man as having to wear woollen underwear in the wintertime and had to pay on that woollen underwear a sales tax of three per cent. He said that the poor man also had to wear a suit of woollen clothes, and asked: Mr. Speaker, do you realize that a man who pays $30 for a suit of woollen clothes has to pay 90 cents in the shape of this "iniquitous sales tax" to the government? He said the sales tax was a war tax and should have been abolished long ago. Well, the war was over ten years at that time, and it is over sixteen years now, and the sales tax is still on, but the man who buys a $30 suit of woollen clothes is not paying only 90 cents to the government to-day; he pays $1.80 under the taxation imposed by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. Before the King government went out of power the tax had been reduced to one per cent and the tax on the suit of clothes was only 30 cents, but the sales tax is still here, the iniquitous sales tax which my hon. friend the present Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) proposed to have removed. This iniquitous sales tax and the poor man's income tax is still here and has been multiplied by six under the present government.
The financing of maturing obligations-that was a study which my right hon. friend the Prime Minister had dealt with on successive occasions that might have been introduced into the present budget as something out of the ordinary. The sinking fund he proposed at first, and then later he suggested when he was in opposition over on this side of the house that there should be some way of converting the national debt. Hon. members will recall that he mentioned it when he was speaking in the debate the other night on the motion that the Speaker leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply. When he was in opposition he advocated that there should be issued four per cent Canadian consols, and that the insurance companies and the banks should be compelled to subscribe for these consols and retire the national debt. This is what he said in 1927 in Hansard at page 407:
If my suggestion were carried out there would be some diminution in interest profits, but in view of the fact that there are such vast profits earned over and above the money necessary to take care of reserves at three and three and a half per cent, no hardship 
would be imposed upon the Canadian people, who would realize that their savings, although the profits of the life insurance companies might be affected-and as my hon. friend knows, life insurance is intended for protection rather than for profit-would be available for the whole of the people, while the trusteeship obligation imposed on the companies would be better discharged by reason of the stability and certainty of the securities.
At that time my right hon. friend did not indicate that there was any difficulty at all about reducing the income of the life insurance companies, but in speaking in this house the other evening, as reported at page 1629 of Hansard, and I have read each passage that makes any reference to the life insurance companies, he studiously avoids altogether the views which he expressed in 1927. The most he says is on page 1629 where he says:
Who are the holders of these securities? They are primarily the insurance companies, primarily those who, for the purpose of meeting contracts maturing in the future, have invested in these securities on the basis of their yielding somewhat a higher rate than three and a half per cent to take care of contingent losses that may arise by reason of fortuitous circumstances. Every hon. member, if he will think for just a moment, will realize, will understand that.
I say, Mr. Speaker, it is remarkable what a difference the responsibilities of office make. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister in 1927, when he was in opposition, thought there was no difficulty at all in forcing the life insurance companies and the banks to subscribe to four per cent securities. But it is a very different thing in 1934, when the suggestion is made that perhaps these insurance companies might head a campaign for the lowering of interest rates in this country and for the converting of the national debt. No, Mr. Speaker, that proposal is not in the budget. The beaten track is not left so far as debt conversion is concerned.
There is another thing. I felt that in the budget this year we might at least have heard of a promise that was made by the Prime Minister in 1930, and I quoted that promise the first time I spoke on the budget after the 1930 election. There were a good many promises made by the Prime Minister. There was one made down in the province of Nova Scotia by the Prime Minister with regard to old age pensions. The promise was contained in a letter which I put on record at that time, and which I shall not quote in full to-day, but from which I will extract a couple of paragraphs:

Bennett's Pledge On Old Age Pensions Conservative Federal Headquarters Victoria Building 140 Wellington Street Redmond Code,
General Secretary.
Ottawa, Canada.
July 12, 1930.
To the people of Nova Scotia:
I leave out the first two paragraphs. The third paragraph reads:
While the old people of your province were unable to benefit by the present act during the last two years, nevertheless through the contribution of one-half of the pension money from the federal treasury you have been contributing your share of the pension money going to the old people in other provinces. This situation cannot continue.
Mr. King says that in order to adopt a national old age pension bill, we will have to amend the British North America Act as it is now unconstitutional for the federal government to pass such a bill. I contend that if the dominion government can contribute 50 per cent as they do at present, they can contribute it all.
If returned to power on the 28th of this month, I pledge my party to pass a national old age pension bill by which the federal treasury will provide all the money required- thus treating all the old people alike, whether they live in the maritimes or in any other part of Canada.
Faithfully yours,
R. B. Bennett,
Leader Liberal-Conservative Party.
I directed the attention of the right hon. Prime Minister to that promise ten months after the Conservative party came into power; I said it seemed to me that the old people of the province of Nova Scotia had a right, after that letter had been sent to them two weeks before the election, to believe that as soon as possible after the Conservative party were in power the 100 per cent old age pension act would be passed, because it is not very much good promising old people an old age pension act and then waiting three or four years to pass it; a good many of those to whom the promise was made would not live to get the benefit of it. At that time the Prime Minister said it was not promised that the act would be passed immediately, and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) interrupted and said " It will be done." I would point out to the Minister of Justice that it is now two years and ten months since he made that statement in the house and that it is now three years and nine months since the letter was written, but the promise of a one hundred per cent old age pension act is still unfulfilled. So I ask my hon. friends, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) for the sake of the Minister of Trade and (Commerce (Mr. The Budget-Mr. Ralston
Stevens):	How about just breaking away
from the beaten track for once and fulfilling just one promise? How about just breaking away from the track that seems to have been laid down by the party opposite, of disregarding promises entirely, and fulfilling just this one promise? But that has not been done. Apparently there is only one beaten track for my hon. friends as far as budgets are concerned; that is debt, deficits and taxes. There is nothing else, and so far as any features go which would satisfy the ambitions, the desires and the ardour of my friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, this budget is just as featureless as the Sahara desert; the only thing in it is this tax on gold, to which I shall refer in a few moments.
_ There is something else to which I should like to refer. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance, as I can understand, has to be guilty of a certain amount of repetition in connection with his budget speeches, but there is one phrase I do hope he will omit if he happens to bring down a budget next year, that is to say if .there has not been an election in the meantime. I find that in 1932 almost the last words in my hon. friend's budget address were:
As a final word, may I say that I do not propose to indulge in prophecy. But I do desire to record my firm conviction that we are not far removed from events which will herald the dawn of better days-
That address was delivered on April 6, 1932, and the results that year showed a deficit of $157,700,000 and an addition to the debt of $148,126,000, together with additional taxes, as will be remembered by hon. members of this house and by the country, so that the better days did not dawn. Then in 1933 my hon. friend used these words in concluding his remarks :
At the same time we have no occasion to despair for the future. On the contrary I am of the firm belief that we can look forward with complete confidence to better and happier days.
In that year, according to the budget which my hon. friend has just brought down, we had a total deficit of $135,200,000, an increase in the debt of $139,244,000 and now we have this tax on gold, to which I am going to refer shortly. The better and happier days are still deferred. Now this year, in 1934, I find my hon. friend still optimistic; he says:
May we with renewed hope, fresh courage and firm step press on towards the goal of better and happier days which lie not far ahead.
I believe my hon. friend spoke better than he knew this time; I really believe the better and happier days are going to come, if there
2426	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Ralston
is an election. My hon. friend evidently was thinking of Nova Scotia, of British Columbia, of Restigouche-Madawaska, of Yamaska, of South Huron, of Mackenzie and of South Oxford. Judging from the example that has been given by these constituencies my hon. friend, I feel satisfied, can look forward to better and happier days under Liberal government. If there were to be no election and the present government remained in power I would say that I should set these words of his to music, to the tune of "The same old story in the same old way," but if the election comes off, as we hope it will, the tune can more suitably be, " Happy days are here again."
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to refer to some matters which are in the budget, not matters which are left out but matters included in the budget. The first to which I intend to refer-and it is not new to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance or to this house-is the fact that notwithstanding all that has been said in the past by the right hon. Prime Minister, this is not a budget. The matters which are not in this budget, so far as a list of expenditures is concerned, are rather formidable. We have understood that in the budget there should be brought down a statement of the expenditures made during the last fiscal year, a review of trade conditions, an indication of the government's policy with regard to trade, and a forecast of what conditions were to be expected during the coming year, together with the financial commitments which are to be made. I find fault with this budget on two grounds, first the items which are omitted and secondly the predictions which have proved grossly inaccurate. I cite as my authority for the necessity of compliance with those two principles the right hon. Prime Minister himself, who in 1931 condemned in unmeasured terms the former Minister of Finance for not having predicted a deficit of $75,000,000, indicating that this was:
the basis of responsible government, it is the basis upon which representative institutions have been established, and that responsibility can only attach when there is some estimate as to what is being received by the country from the taxation imposed and as to what expenditures are to be made.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, in the light of these words, if this is a budget.	,
In this budget is there any estimate for the so called public works program that is supposed to come down some of these days? Is it not proper that this should be included somewhere in the budget? I have looked through it from end to end, and the only statements I can find

with regard to any expenses other than ordinary expenses are simply a reference to relief and a reference to a deficit on the Canadian National Railways. There is no statement here with regard to public works, though we understand that the amount to be spent will be something like $50,000,000. Is there anything here for advances under the relief bill other than the ordinary advances which have been made from year to year and which, unfortunately, we are coming to regard as ordinary though they are most extraordinary because they are made under the authority of a blank cheque. There is nothing whatever in this budget with regard to them. My hon. friend does not even deign to give the amount which will be spent for relief; neither does he deign to give the amount which he thinks will be spent in connection with the Canadian National. Is there anything here to show the amount involved if the wheat obligation should come due this year? Is there anything to indicate the amount which would have to be provided to pay that? Not a dollar. That is not in the accounts at all. All that my hon. friend does is attempt to raise enough money to pay the ordinary expenditures which he knows about, to comfort himself with the idea that there might be $8,000,000 surplus on ordinary account and then let the future take care of itself. I submit that that is not a budget which will meet any test as to the necessities of a budget. It is not a budget which would meet the requirements laid down only two or three years ago in this House of Commons by the Prime Minister.
But further than that, it is not a budget because it shows, as have previous budgets, that there has been an absolutely inaccurate estimate of the necessities of the public service. Let me speak about the item I have just mentioned. In 1933 my hon. friend estimated $35,000,000 for special expenditures and non-active advances. What did he spend? He spent $52,570,000 or $17,570,000_ more. He estimated for the Canadian National Railways $47,941,000 and spent $52,264,000, leaving out entirely the eastern lines deficits. In other words, there is a difference of over $22,000,000 on those two items. My hon. friend may take whichever horn of the dilemma he likes. If his leader was right when he said that the Chancellor of the Exchequer in delivering his budget address in the British parliament is always held to the strictest account as to the extent to which he has been able to realize his expectations and the extent to which his representations agree with the facts of the year in review-if I say his right hon.

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
leader was right at that time, then my hon. friend stands condemned out of the mouth of his leader himself.
As the years go by under this government we are getting farther and farther away from the first principles of government. We are getting to the stage where power is being handed over to the sixteen or seventeen men sitting on the treasury benches and this House of Commons is told simply to give a blank cheque, to give them not only the power of parliament but the resources of the treasury as well.
Then, so far as this year's budget is concerned, let me remind my hon. friend of the predictions which have been made in the past, and how far short they have fallen. In 1931 the right hon. Prime Minister, then acting as Minister of Finance, said, speaking about the probable customs duties which he had taken into consideration in estimating his budget:
Taking this into consideration the figures presented' indicate a balancing of the budget by a substantial margin in respect of expenditures properly applicable to 1931-32, after excluding capital.
He said they indicated a balancing of the budget by a substantial margin. When the accounts were cast up and my hon. friend the present Minister of Finance had to present the budget in the following year to the house the so-called balancing of the budget by a substantial margin had faded into insignificance, and my right hon. friend, the Prime Minister's estimate of revenue was $71,652,000 too optimistic, and instead of the budget being balanced there was a deficit of $81,000,000. In 1932 my hon. friend cautiously, as befitted a new Minister of Finance, referring to revenues from customs and excise taxes said:
Without building too greatly on help from these sources in the present year it is the considered view of the government that reductions in expenditure on the one hand, and proposed additions to the taxation revenues on the other, will in the final outcome represent a complete balancing of the budget on the usual governmental services.
Yet we find the result of the year's financing was not the balancing of the budget, but a deficit on ordinary account alone of $53,000,000. Then again in 1933, I shall read the minister's remarks as they appear in Hansard for 1933, page 3223:
Accordingly it is proposed to recommend measures which will, it is anticipated, produce at least $70,000,000 on the basis of present business conditions, leaving a surplus of $2,000,000. Even a slight improvement in price levels and the general volume of business would increase substantially the surplus to be applied against capital and special expenditures.
But when we look at the budget speech which the finance minister has just delivered we find that the $2,000,000 surplus he predicted has turned out to be a $24,000,000 deficit notwithstanding that business has improved' as he says.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that those are not budgets in the sense, at least, in which his right hon. leader understands them. I am afraid that predicting in this country is becoming a sort of byword. It is shaking the confidence of the people in their government. I would not mind so much if the Prime Minister had not adopted that holier than thou attitude, had not wrapped a mantle of purity about him and given thanks that he was not as other men were, and indicated that he was the only man who had ever brought down a real budget. But having done that and having plumed himself on his own righteousness then he ought to be held to it. I submit that having boasted of his own rectitude of deportment the Prime Minister and his Minister of Finance stand convicted of the very offence which the right hon. gentleman has charged against others, only in a greater degree, namely that of omitting entirely items which should be in the budget and consequently failing by millions of dollars properly to predict the result of the year's financial operations. For the consideration of the Prime Minister I suggest that instead of giving lectures to other people on budget making he might, it seems to me, having regard to that record, take a correspondence course himself in that subject.
For a moment or two I should like to deal with the matter of public debt. The Minister of Finance has not placed on record any indication of the public debt except that pertaining to the present year. I realize he is not required to do it, but it seems to me that such a table would have been informative. At the risk of detaining this house I shall read into the record figures showing what the public debt has been in each year, beginning with the fiscal year of March 31, 1930:

These figures show a total increase between March 31, 1930, and March 31, 1934, of

The Budget-Mr. Ralston

$594,405,000. That means an increase in the interest payable by the people of this country of practically $25,000,000 per year, or $2.50 per head. That is the interest load which has been put on the people of Canada since this government took office. As will be remembered, under the old Liberal government, between the years 1925 and 1930 there was recorded a total surplus of $257,000,000.
My hon. friend may say that this government's position is due to railway deficits. Let me remind him that during the Liberal administration current deficits on railways were paid out of revenue, and were not added to the public debt. Let me remind him, further, that under the Conservative government between the years 1919 and 1921 the average deficit on railways before paying interest due the public averaged $22,000,000 yearly. From 1922 to 1930 under Liberal government the average surplus available for payment of interest due to the public was $24,000,000, and the deficits began again in 1931 under the present government with $4,100,000 and for the last two years over $3,000,000 each year before paying interest due to the public.
Someone else may say that the debt is due to relief. Well, Mr. Speaker, relief was not contemplated when this government came into office. There was to be no relief. There was to be no necessity for relief. Speaking in this house the Prime Minister realized that conditions were serious in 1930. Before he went down to Moncton and made his promise, the Prime Minister made a statement which appears on page 18 of Hansard of 1930. He said:
What about conditions in this dominion at this moment? What about conditions from east to west? It is true that part of the unemployment is seasonal; but since the beginning of the year I have traversed Canada from Victoria to the far east, and in every city of this dominion, east and west, there is abnormal unemployment, so that men who are accustomed to give, as I have been, to assist those who are unable to earn sufficient to keep body and soul together, have never before seen such distress as I have seen in the communities I have visited'.
Then he went down to Moncton and said that he would give work to every man who was willing to work, or perish in the attempt; that he would give work, not doles. He cannot say he did not know what the conditions were at that time, and he promised that employment would be found. The public debt has been increased by $596,000,000; the increased interest charges amount to $25,000,000 a year or $2.50 for every man, woman and child in the dominion. I should like to put on record the Moncton promise of the Prime Minister because it seems to me that this goes with

the passage I have just read. The promise was:
The Conservative party is going to find work for all who are willing to work, or perish in the attempt. It is going to call parliament at the earliest possible date after July 28, and take such steps as will end this tragic condition of unemployment and bring prosperity to the country as a whole. . . . Mr. King promises consideration of the problems of unemployment. I promise to end unemployment. Which plan do you like best?
In bringing down his budget this year the Minister of Finance strikes rather an optimistic note in the first paragraph or two of his speech. He indicates that statistics show that conditions in this country are improving a little but he does not say anything about the fact that at the end of February there were still receiving relief heads of families totalling 267.853, while the total on relief numbered 1,270,599. I place those figures beside the statement of the Prime Minister at Moncton in 1930. My hon. friend must produce more than statistics furnished by the bureau of statistics to convince the people of Canada that at the present time all is well in the dominion. You do not need to take index figures or adjusted trade returns, all you have to do is to go up and down and across the length and breadth of this country to find that there is still a lot to be done in the way of improving conditions before we get back to the days we had before 1930.
Let me now deal with the matter of debt conversion. The other night the Prime Minister referred to this in the debate which arose on the motion to go into supply. I believe that the development of trade, the balancing of the budget and the conversion of our debt are the three most important questions in this country. The Prime Minister has given the impression that we must all stand still until 1937 has passed as far as the conversion of the debt is concerned. He says that the letter of the bond is there and that it must be observed. The Minister of Finance says that the sole remedy with regard to the conversion of the public debt or the easing of the burden of the public debt is a rise in the price level. I would hardly think that the taxing of gold is a good way to raise the price level, but my hon. friend knows best. The interest burden is now $139,730,000, while this year's deficit will add another $6,000,000 making the total $145,000,000 per year. In his budget speech the Minister of Finance said that the Prime Minister had dealt with the matter of debt conversion. I submit that a matter as important as this one deserves more than an offhand statement from the Prime Minister in a debate on a motion to go into supply; I

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
submit that it deserves detailed attention in the budget speech. I do not profess to offer anything new but I would remind the Minister of Finance that in 1928 the Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, said this:
Is this country to continue to be menaced by this economic evil, by this debt hanging over our heads? Are we to continue, of all countries in the world, to make no provision for the future? Are we to be content to expend our patrimony day by day without putting anything aside to take care of the long days of the future that are before us? I say it is unfair to posterity, and still more, it is unfair to ourselves, it is unfair to the taxpayers of this country to extract from them each year these increasingly large sums of money and make no provision for the retirement of our national obligations. The sum to be set aside is not large. I can only say this, that if we on this side of the house were entrusted with power, we would not hesitate a single moment to make provision for the retirement of the national debt of this country.
He continued on page 1251 as follows:
Then why does not the Minister of Finance devote his energies to converting our national debt upon a large scale, instead of reading us some piffling remarks, written by an economist a hundred years ago? Let me go further. The saving of 20 million dollars a year on the refunding of the debt might be possible if you would say to the holders of the 5J per cent tax exempt securities maturing within the next nine and ten years that there would be freedom from or great deduction of income tax during the next decade. Does it ever occur to hon. members that in addition to the 110 million dollars free money, the exemption from income tax for the next five or ten years might bring about a great expansion of public revenue?
I have just one more extract. All this has to do with the conversion of the public debt and with the things the Prime Minister proposed to do at that time. He was impatient with the Minister of Finance of that day and he said that two billions of securities ought to be converted. He is reported on page 1252 as follows:
With two billions of securities maturing in nine or ten years, and with money at 4 per cent, there is the greatest opportunity that was ever offered to any minister of finance in this country. To seize that opportunity requires courage, skill, ability, knowledge; it requires willingness to devote some time to a study of the problem. It requires more thought about economies and less inclination to extravagance; it requires more consideration of the question as to how the money is to be secured rather than how it may be spent. It requires the consideration of world factors that determine the price at which money can be obtained. Is this government giving the problem that degree of attention? Is there any evidence of such consideration of the question on their part? Let hon. gentlemen opposite ask themselves that question.
That was in 1928, and we now have an offhand statement by the Prime Minister say-
74726- 154J
ing that he has thought about this question a great deal but has come to the conclusion that 1937 is the earliest time at which we can think of any possible conversion of this debt. As a very humble member of this house let me suggest to him that the first thing to be done in connection with the conversion of our national debt or the lowering of the interest burden is a considered and serious drive towards balancing the budget. If he considered that 1928 when money was cheap at 4 or 4^ per cent was a good time to convert, it seems to me that the present cheapness of money should be taken advantage of. The next thing is a planned major refunding operation, preceded by conferences with institutions and carried out in a manner similar to the victory loan campaign.
The Prime Minister says that there are difficulties with regard to foreign holdings. Possibly there are, but this government has not hesitated to tax non-residents with regard to dividends. The government of the United States has not hesitated-you may call it repudiation or whatever you like-to change the letter of their bond as far as payment in gold is concerned. The Minister of Finance has not hesitated to take advantage of the fact that the United States is regarding its dollar as worth only sixty cents in gold and to make our dollar worth the same. Nothing is said about repudiation when we are paying in these sixty-cent dollars. It seems to me that perhaps we are not meeting the situation fairly when we talk about repudiation and hold up that bogey with regard to debt conversion. Let us assume that there are difficulties with regard to foreign holders, let us assume with the Prime Minister that we want to maintain our credit-by the way, I do not quite appreciate what good we hope to do by maintaining our credit so far as foreign investment is concerned as there does not seem to be much under this government in which foreigners want to invest except gold mines. The sale to foreigners of industrials in this country has not been heavy under this present government.
But let us assume that we desire to keep our credit unsullied in every respect. May I offer this suggestion, for which I claim no originality, because I observed that it was put forward in a Canadian journal one or two weeks ago, and I have also heard it discussed by others. I mention it now simply in order that it may be on record, and that the government, if they have not considered it, may keep it in mind in connection with the conversion of our debt. That suggestion is this. If you feel that you cannot carry on a major refunding operation simply by reducing inter-
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

est rates and planning a victory loan drive, appealing to the patriotic consciences of Canadian citizens, if you cannot manage it by appealing to the institutions and the citizens of the country, or if you feel that a conversion in this way under present circumstances will not be justified, why not consider the question of compensation for reduction of interest rates by way of increasing capital? I say to the government, consider the matter of amortizing the difference between a 4J per cent bond and a 3J or a 3 per cent bond. Add enough capital to the bond to equal the present worth of'the reduction in interest, covering a period of, say, twenty years. You will then have materially decreased the annual interest charge, and the capital will have been increased by a much smaller sum than the total of the annual interest savings. I note that the estimate was made, in this journal to which I have referred, that refunding $1,500,000,000 on the basis of 2| per cent tax free there would be an increase in capital of $200,000,000, but there would be a decrease in annual charges of $20,000,000. On the other hand, refunding $2,300,000,000, would create a capital addition of about $600,000,000, but at the same time it would mean an annual saving of something like $34,000,000. These are proposals that ought to be considered. The Prime Minister did not mention this plan the other night, and I should like to hear his comment upon it. What I do deplore, however, is the rather dogmatic attitude taken both by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Finance in assuming that this matter of debt conversion is completely out of the picture and that we are absolutely obliged to continue paying $145,000,000 in interest per annum whether we like it or not.
No one proposes the repudiation of obligations, but we cannot accept the statement of the Prime Minister and of the Minister of Finance as absolutely the last word in the matter. I repeat, I consider debt adjustment, a balanced budget and an increase of our trade the three greatest problems before the dominion to-day.
Now, I have spoken of the direct obligation of Canada, which is $2,789,152,000 to-day apart altogether from guarantees. But there are indirect obligations, as the Minister of Finance says in his speech. There are additional guarantees, listed in his budget speech, totalling $82,905,000. There are guarantees on account of the Canadian National Railways harbour commissions and Canadian National Steamships of $993,000,000, or a total of $1,075,905,000 -guarantees in addition to the direct debt itself. What does that mean? In round 
figures, that means a total of $3,890,057,000, as the total obligation of this dominion in respect of guarantees and direct obligations.
I have included in that something not stated in the budget speech; I have included an obligation of $25,000,000 on account of the wheat guarantees. The Prime Minister indicated in the house the other day that this might amount possibly to $15,000,000. Well, in my opinion, neither the Prime Minister nor Mr. John I. McFarland nor any man in this house or in the country can tell us what it will amount to; it is absolutely impossible for anyone to predict it, when you find that 100 million bushels of wheat or more is being held. No one knows exactly, but a very large quantity of wheat is hanging over the market. Now, wheat may be quoted at a certain price to-day; drop any large amount of it on the market and attempt to realize and you will see the bottom fall out of the market; you will see how quickly millions will mount up in the way of losses. So that we cannot make an estimate as to the amount of the possible loss in connection with the wheat guarantee.
Right here I wish to protest once more against the idea of the Prime Minister writing a letter giving an absolutely blank guarantee to the banks of the dominion to back up and finance the operations of any one individual in respect of any undertaking. The least that the Prime Minister could have done, when he wrote that letter, was to limit the obligation to so much money; he should have stipulated some figure. At the present time however there is no limit; not a dollar is mentioned. This means that Mr. McFarland, as head of the cooperative wheat producers, can buy and sell as he thinks proper. The suggestion was made that there might have been a limit, but there is no record of any limit at all, so that he may buy and sell as he thinks fit. He may go to the banks and get money and when the whole transaction is over, when the thing is all washed up, when the wheat has been realized on five or ten years from now, the government of Canada will foot the bill and the people of this country will pay for it.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is one of the reasons why I complain of this not being a budget. The Prime Minister, with all due respect to him, is too fond of signing letters in the name of the people of Canada. He signed a letter, in January, 1931, if I remember rightly, guaranteeing the banks with regard to the wheat pool, and passed an order in council the next September, nine months afterwards. That is not good business, having regard to the size of the transaction and the necessity for carrying on government business in a proper way. In the first place, he

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
did it under an act which stipulated no limit whatever, and which he extracted from the members of this house by force of the government majority-an act which makes no provision at all for any limit in amount or purpose, but empowers the government to loan in connection with anything they like. It is primarily a relief measure but it has developed into everything but that. Now, that is one obligation to which I refer. We do not know exactly what the liability is, nor shall we know until Mr. McFarland is all through.
They say that Mr. McFarland is not gambling, not speculating. Let me put the situation to you, Mr. Speaker. Here was the job that was given him. No. 1: You, Mr. McFarland, are to dispose of the 1930 crop. Well, that seems fairly easy; he can go and sell. But, no; Mr. McFarland, while you are to dispose of the 1930 crop you will not depress the market. So that the next step you will take is this. If you find the market going down in connection with the 1931 or the 1932 crop, step in and buy wheat. In other words, instead of selling you are to buy. What is the result? He was charged with the duty of disposing of the 1930 crop, and to-day, after three years, Mr. McFarland, who was supposed to dispose of the crop of 1930, has succeeded to this extent that he has on hand in the shape of futures, millions of bushels more wheat than he started out with. This means that there will have to be rust in the Argentine or a famine somewhere which may provide an outlet for the disposition of that wheat, and in the meantime we will roll up the cost of carrying the wheat each month and each year.
That I say, Mr. Speaker, is not good business. It is not good business for this country that the government should operate in that way. If they wanted to undertake the obligation they should have come to parliament and submitted an estimate of what it would involve, and should have discussed the whole matter thoroughly on the floor of the house before the writing of that letter.
The guarantee in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway is exactly in the same category in many respects. That transaction was carried out in this way. Discussions were had with the Prime Minister, an intimation having been given that the Canadian Pacific Railway would have difficulty in financing for 1933-34. We are told that no suggestion was made at all that the government should guarantee the loan, but suddenly on May 30 the suggestion came from someone-Mr. Beatty I think-that the government should guarantee the loan. The Prime Minister thinks there may have been a discussion earlier than
that. Parliament prorogued on May 27, 1933, and on May 30 the conference was had between Mr. Beatty and the Prime Minister. The next day, May 31, a letter was given by the Prime Minister that this country would guarantee the obligations of the Canadian Pacific for 1933 and 1934, would guarantee the banks so that they might loan money enough to retire those obligations and carry them for the railway for five years. That amounted to $60,000,000. When was the order in council passed in respect to that? The following November, November 29, 1933. This was a good thing for the Canadian Pacific, so far as financing was concerned; the banks got a good piece of business, but the Prime Minister is too prone to sign his name to letters, to doing things in a big way and using the credit of the Dominion of Canada for that purpose. I am reminded that the money was loaned and the advances made by the banks all through the summer of 1933 long before the order in council was passed. That is the situation. What has happened? We are talking about four and a half per cent or four per cent loans for the Dominion of Canada. What are the banks getting out of the Canadian Pacific guarantees? A guarantee of interest at five per cent with practically a government bond backing it up, because it is a letter of the Prime Minister of Canada backed up by an order in council. What are the banks getting with regard to the wheat pool? The dominion can borrow at four or four and a half per cent, but the banks are getting five and a half per cent for the wheat pool borrowings under a dominion guarantee. I want to be fair to the banks; they are giving four per cent on money left on deposit, but five and a half per cent is the rate paid to the banks by the cooperative wheat producers and that despite the fact that they have a government guarantee behind them.

I was quite satisfied it was five and one-half per cent. I accept my hon. friend's correction if that is so, but as a matter of fact I think it is five and one-half per cent. It is, however, a rate above that which the Dominion of Canada should be paying for guaranteeing the banks or anybody else for money.
Further, with regard to the Canadian Pacific loan, let me say this. The statement is made and is unchallenged that the loan which the Bank of Montreal made to the Canadian Pacific they were willing to carry on the security which they had without any dominion guarantee. In some way or another the Prime Minister felt that the matter was
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

important enough for him to intervene and apparently the suggestion came from him just as much as it did from anybody else, that the five-year financing be done now and that the government step in like a great father, take over the whole load of the Canadian Pacific financing for the next two years and give this blanket guarantee. Those are matters which do not appear in the budget speech. The $60,000,000 guarantee is there, but the circumstances under which it is made do not appear in the budget and are not mentioned by the Minister of Finance in his speech. So, if we take the guarantees both direct and indirect and add the $50,000,000 to be spent in public works we find that the national debt is something more like $4,000,000,000 than the $2,700,000,000 which was mentioned by my hon. friend. So much for the blue side of the sheet so far as the book-keeping is concerned.
I feel that the Minister of Finance has not done quite justice to himself or to the country or to the government in the way in which he has presented in his budget the trade figures and the business of the dominion. He does not seem to realize that perhaps the most important thing in this country is trade; that we cannot collect any taxes, that we cannot hope to get rid of our railway debt or our other debts and deficits unless we have trade. But in a budget speech which occupies twenty-seven pages of Hansard, two pages are devoted to trade and the figures in connection with it. A budget should present some study of the trend of trade in this country of the various classes who are doing business here, of the possible avenues of trade and of the possibilities of developing the trade which we have. I find in the budget what I think is most fragmentary information. We have the total trade of Canada for the fiscal year; the comparative total trade from 1930 to 1934; the intra-empire trade for a year; comparisons between empire and United States imports and exports, and the only reference to international trade outside the United Kingdom is the total increase and the balance of trade. That is not enough for a budget speech of the Dominion of Canada; we ought to have a serious attempt to show exactly the condition of trade in this country and the possibilities of its development.
Anything there is in the budget speech with regard to trade seems to be aimed at this object and this only-to try, if possible, to justify the government's policy with respect to the shackling of trade and the imperial conference agreements. That seems to be as far 
as they go. The only reference which is made is this, and I am quoting:
The beneficial effects of the empire trade agreements are shown in the expansion of intra-empire trade.
The minister winds up with this statement:
These developments in our external trade have been distinctly favourable, reflecting the soundness^ of the policies which have been pursued in connection with the trade agreements, and testifying_ to the stability and efficiency of Canadian industry.
Again the trade agreements have been particularly mentioned. What are the facts? In the first place, with regard to the trade agreements and trade with the empire, as I tried to point out before in the house, the tendency is that way anyway; my hon. friends cannot get any credit because of the fact they happen to have these trade agreements signed in 1932, because the tendency of trade since 1930 and before has been for empire trade.

speechtext:
My hon. friends laugh. I have in my hand a publication issued under the authority of the present Minister of Trade and Commerce:	Canada's Foreign Trade,
1933, and at page 15 it states:
The tendency of Canada's trade quite apart from the trade agreements during the past three or four years has been toward a greater exchange of commodities with empire countries.
This was natural. In the last year the tendency has been more marked than ever. Why? Because of the rise in sterling, because of the increased purchasing power of British money; second, because of the prosperity of the British people and their getting back into the purchasing world again.. Yet my hon. friend turns this to his own account and says that the trade agreements have brought about this increase. The fact of the matter is that any increase in trade between Canada and the mother country has been due to natural and economic causes.

But the hon. member
nevertheless voted against the tendency.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I did not vote against the tendency; I voted against my hon. friends pegging the tariff on 139 different articles in order to prevent trade with the rest of the world.
Let me point out what the statement of the Minister of Finance says with regard to the increase in trade. I take his own figures. I do not know that they are even as enthusiastic as the tendency indicated by the publication issued by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I find this on page 2274 of Hansard: if we take the proportion of our exports

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
which went to the British Empire in the eleven months ended February 28,	1934,
over those of the same period in 1933, they increased by the astounding percentage of -83 per cent. That is exactly what my right hon. friend shows; in 1933 it was 46-83 per cent- I am reading from his own speech-and in 1934 it was 47-66 per cent. Now the proportion of our exports which went to the United States in that same period, according to the same statement-and this is the policy which according to him vindicates the tendency and the soundness of the policies of the government regarding empire agreements-increased by 3-03 per cent; in other words nearly four times as much increase to the United States.
As to imports, the proportion of our imports which came from the British Empire increased by 4-37 per cent; the proportion of our imports which came from the United States decreased by 3-18 per cent. Now let us see where the principle of bargaining comes in.
The basic principle of this government's policy was that you must bargain; you must get a quid for your quo every time. But the result of these figures is this; For the year ending March 31, 1934 we bought 3-7 per cent more of our imports from Britain than in 1933 and we sold them only -83 per cent more of our exports. In other words, we increased our imports from them four times as much as they increased their imports from us. That is the quid pro quo we got as the result of our bargaining.
When my hon. friends opposite talk about bargaining, let us go back to the period from 1921 to 1930. The amount we sold from 1921 to 1930 to Britain and the empire was $4,057,000,000, when we did not have any Ottawa agreements at all to encourage any tendency or vindicate any soundness of policy. We sold them $4,057,000,000, and we bought from them only $1,823,000,000. Yet hon. gentlemen opposite know, and I am sure that some of them are perhaps shivering a bit now, particularly those who represent agricultural counties, that there is going to be an attempt made to revise the British trade agreements in June of this year. My hon. friends are going to find out that the three year schedule on certain agricultural commodities will be running out and that there is going to be an attempt made, as has already been indicated in the newspapers, to revise the schedules particularly with regard to agricultural products.
What about wheat? Wheat was the thing on which we were going to get a preference. The imperial conference agreements were going to be a great help to wheat. I quote Broomhall, March 10, 1934, showing the imports into Great Britain of wheat. The imports from Roumania in the season August 1,

Now, what else? He did not look over on the other side of the page and tell us what our imports from New Zealand were. While our exports to New Zealand have increased by 6 per cent, our imports from New Zealand have increased by 148 per cent. I wondered what it could be that we were importing from New Zealand at this time.

I do not want to pursue that very much further, except that I want to put on record what is not on record in the budget speech, namely the record of Canada's total trade, because we on this side of the house, regardless of what hon. gentlemen opposite are interested in, still believe in trade not only with the British Empire but with the world at large. So my hon. friend the Minister of Finance puts it rather prominently in his budget speech that there has been an increase in total trade, from 1933 to 1934, of $132,000,000. Well, it is pretty easy to get an increase if you start at the lowest point, which in this case is 1933. That was the lowest point in the trade of Canada since 1912, so it is possible to show some increase, and I am very glad indeed that this increase has come about. It is just the same as a patient with a temperature of 105; if that temperature gets down to 1044 the patient is improving, no doubt, but even under those conditions the patient is not altogether well.

The serious thing, however, according to the Prime Minister's past statements is this: I do not know anybody who talked as much about the Canadian people being hewers of wood and drawers of water and the exporting of our raw materials as the Prime Minister when he sat here as leader of the opposition. Will you believe me, Mr. Speaker, when I say that on looking up the record of this government I find that whereas in 1930 our exports of raw materials totalled 38 per cent of all our exports-and that was when my hon. friend was travelling all over this country criticizing us-in the year covered by this budget raw materials amounted to 45 per cent of our total exports. Hewers of wood; draw-

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
ers of water; giving away our patrimony; selling our inheritance for a mess of pottage- these were the expressions used in 1930 while to-day, under the gentleman who said so much about it in 1930, we have a 20 per cent increase in our exports of raw materials.
Now for a moment I should like to deal with farm products, and. I think it will be agreed that some of these things should be dealt with in connection with the budget. The important feature to the people of this country perhaps is not so much the export of industrial goods or manufactured articles as it is the export of agricultural products, the products of the farm, the forest, the sea, and the mine. I find that notwithstanding the increase of $105,000,000 in exports, in 1931 the exports of agricultural products totalled $209,000,000; in 1932 they totalled $204,000,000 and in 1933 they amounted to only $198,000,000. In other words the increase in exports, which my hon. friend gave as $105,000,000, has not taken place in connection with farm products, but instead there has been a falling off. That brings me directly to this point: We are trying to assist in arriving at some kind of parity between the price level of agricultural and other primary products and the price level of other commodities. How are we getting on? In presenting his budget speech my hon. friend the Minister of Finance congratulated himself, I think, and this country on the fact that while the wholesale price index was rising by 13-4 per cent the index of farm products rose 34-9 per cent. But those are percentages of increase, not actual increases of the index figure; they do not indicate, as one might think, that the index figure rose by 34-9. In the first place the increase is due to the fact that, as in connection with the total trade of Canada, the minister started at the lowest point, which I think was February, 1933. Let me read to you what the position is with regard to the relative position of price levels as between agricultural and primary products and other commodities from 1930 right up to the present; time.

I am afraid my friend the Minister of Finance cannot give much comfort to the farmers by saying there has been an increase in the price level of primary products as compared with the general commodity price level. The point is that there is still that disparity of almost 20 points between those two price levels, and we will not have prosperity in this country until that gap is more nearly closed up.
The Minister of Finance mentioned the balance of trade. Wc have dealt with that on so many occasions that I need only take a moment at this time. My hon. friend rejoices in the fact that there is an excess of exports over imports of $142,000,000, and he says that does not take account of the export of gold, amounting to $90,000,000, thus intimating that there is a total favourable balance of trade of $232,000,000. Here again this publication put out by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce does not seem to jibe with the statement of the Minister of Finance. I have in my hand an extract from a publication called Estimated Balance of International Payments of Canada, published by the Hon, H. H. Stevens, M. P., Minister of Trade and Commerce, Ottawa. Here I find a statement of the estimated balance, but it is not $232,000,000. Leaving out the detailed items I give the last two debits and credits. The exports are given as $1,216,200,000; the imports are given as $1,114,200, leaving a difference not of $232,000,000 as the Minister of Finance would suggest but of $102,000,000. Of course that is a difference of only $130,000,000, but what is that between friends? As a matter of fact the bureau of statistics, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce knows, regards this balance of trade as something of a fantasy; they have an idea that trade always balances eventually, that the total international payments balance, and they do rather a remarkable and, so far as the Minister of Finance is concerned, a shocking thing when they come to show the balance of trade at $102,000,000. Do you know what entry they make? They say, "Net errors and omissions, $102,000,000." They do that in order to balance up, because they do not regard this as a real balance at all. Of course, my hon. friend knows that the bureau of statistics, in publishing its statement covering 1926 to 1932, said:
Balance of trade figures are frequently misinterpreted due to the persistence of the doctrine, long ago exploded, that a nation's trade is necessarily in a healthy state when exports exceed imports, necessitating an import of gold to make up the difference.
So we do not get much comfort out of that balance of trade. I have said before and I repeat that if you get a balance of trade by starving yourself, by restricting your imports or by not getting the things you should get in order that you may be comfortable, that you may have the necessities and perhaps even
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

some luxuries, then that favourable balance of trade is a bad thing. On the other hand, if the favourable balance is made up by increasing your exports while you are supplying your own necessities, by supplying the world at large and being able, from your abundance, to import, then the favourable balance of trade is a good thing. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that a favourable balance of trade which is produced by privation, by having to buy less, is not a good thing; the favourable balance of trade in which we all rejoice is the balance produced by the exhilaration of being able to sell more.
Now let me say a further word; I am still on trade, but I cannot leave this point, because it seems to me this is a state of affairs which even some of my hon. friends opposite do not seem to realize. What has this government done with regard to the increasing of the foreign trade of this country? I have already dealt with the imperial conference agreements amd with the statements of the Minister of Finance in regard thereto. Let us now have a look at my friends' activities as the champion trade agreement makers. These hon. members opposite are the men who are really supposed to know how to make trade agreements and who, according to their own statements, have negotiated several very valuable ones. Of course, they frowned on the agreement with France made by the Liberal government; they said that was a poor agreement, one which worked against Canadian interests, and for that reason they cancelled it. They made agreements-how many do you say? They made three, outside of the imperial conference agreements. One was with Germany, another with Austria and the third with France.
Let us now see how much trade they have developed through their trade treaties. The order in council authorizing the treaty with Germany was passed March 31, 1933. In 1932 the exports to Germany were $7,700,000. In 1933 the exports to that country were $9,900,000, showing an increase in exports of about $2,000,000. If hon. members will take the trouble to look into those figures they will find that the exports making up the difference were largely wheat and metals, commodities which Germany needed. At the same time, however, there was an increase of $2,000,000 in exports to Germany, with imports remaining about the same.
Now, let us turn to France. That, by the way, is the treaty where a great improvement was supposed to have been made. In 1932 our exports to France were $14,000,000, while in 1933 our exports were $12,200,000. That is a falling off, instead of an increase in exports.

The old treaty expired in June, 1932, and because of that I have compiled the figures for a six months' period. I find that in the last six months operating under the old treaty we exported $8,500,000 of goods to France, while in 1932 when we had no treaty we exported $5,000,000. Then, in 1933, under this brand new, shining treaty of my hon. friends opposite we exported $6,600,000, or in other words $2,000,000 less than was exported under the old treaty.
What is the summary of the treaties and trade agreements negotiated by the present government? The summary is this: They sold $2,000,000 more to Germany than we did the year before the treaty was made, and $2,000,000 less to France. Oh yes, but there is another treaty to be considered-Austria; we have a treaty with Austria. Let us see what our trade with Austria has been. In
1932	exports to Austria were $8,900, and in
1933	under the treaty they were $13,900. In other words, there has been an increase of $5,000. To summarize, there is an increase of $2,000,000 to Germany, a decrease of $2,000,000 to France, and an increase of $5,000 to Austria. That is the contribution which my hon. friends opposite have made to world trade by their trade agreements.
Now, one thing more. Hon. members opposite have always been very keen, and laudably so, to show that Canada is doing better than anybody else. If that were true nothing could give us greater pride. However I feel that we ought to look at the facts, and see if my hon. friends opposite are correct in their assumption, because if Canada is not doing as well as other nations we should know it. I have before me three tables. May I state that I believe we are more deeply interested in exports. I have had a table prepared, taking the year 1928 as a basis, because I thought that was a fair year. The exports of each country for 1928 have been taken at 100 and then a comparison is made with the exports of 1933. With that in mind I have made up the index figure for 1933 representing exports of each country as compared with 1928 which I have taken as 100. They are as follows:

So hon. members opposite will have to look to their export trade more than they have been doing if they wish to show that as compared with the figures for 1928 Canada is increasing her export position. As my hon. friends opposite like to take the low points, let us compare the export figures for 1932 as compared with those for 1933. In these foreign trade figures showing increases in exports of 1933 over those of 1932 we find that Canada is sixteenth on the list . Australia is first with a percentage of 35, and Canada sixteenth with the figure 7-6. That is Canada's position in increases in exports as compared with 1932.
We have always boasted that Canada has been fifth in total world trade. She did hold that position in 1930. In 1932 however Canada was seventh and in 1933 she took ninth position. Last year, Canada's export position was fifth, and this year she is sixth. In imports Canada was last year in eighth position and this year she is in ninth.
The point I am trying to drive home, if I can, by the use of these figures is this, that my hon. friends opposite have completely neglected the development of world trade. In the first place, they are shutting themselves in behind a tariff wall, and in the next place they have adopted some sort of economic imperialism which seems to be filling their hearts and minds, a policy which I am afraid is going to prove a delusion. They are neglecting the opportunity-because there is an opportunity-to develop trade with the world at large. The figures show it, and I commend them to the consideration, of my hon. friends the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I had intended at this point to deal with the matter of revenues, but I do feel that I ought to bring home to the Minister of Finance the point which I have made before but which, like some other points I have made, he does not seem to have caught. I refer to my suggestion of making customs duties a source of greater revenue than they are at present. I have pointed out to my hon. friend that in past years customs duties have been used to good effect in producing revenue which could be used to run the services of the country. The following figures will serve to indicate the percentage of our total revenues made up by customs duties:
