And this year, I am sorry to say, only 24 per cent of the total revenues collected was made up of customs duties. Why? Because my hon. friends opposite have put up such high tariffs that they have virtually created an embargo, with the result that goods do not come in and therefore are not subject to duty. He is feeling the effects of the law of diminishing returns. As I pointed out at the beginning of my remarks, he cannot possibly overtake the diminution of customs tariffs. In 1931 the Prime Minister said he was going to secure a certain revenue from customs duties. However he was $22,000,000 short, because at the special session of 1930 he raised the tariffs. In 1932 the present Minister of Finance guessed he was going to get $100,000,000 from customs duties, and received only $80,000,000, because of higher duties imposed. In 1933 my friend guessed again and said that $72,000,000 was the most he could expect from customs duties and, owing to the increases in tariff which had taken place, as I said a while ago, he received not $72,000,000 but $65,900,000. All this is in spite of what my hon. friend calls expanding trade. All this is in spite of the fact that according to hon. members opposite the country is doing better. The fact is that our revenue from customs duties is going down.
Let me give my hon. friend an example of how the duties that they have put on have hurt our exports. This government put on sharp increases of tariff against the United States. The United States put on an import tax of $3 and a duty of $1 against our lumber. The result was an imposition of four dollars against us. We then to find a market for our lumber included it in our treaty with Great Britain. What has occurred in connection with our timber exports to the United States due to the high duties which were put on against that country? In 1930 we exported to the United States $26,000,000 worth of planks and boards; in 1933 we exported only $6,000,000 worth of planks and boards, a drop of $20,000,000. My hon. friends think we got a market in the United Kingdom. In 1930 we exported to the United Kingdom $5,500,000 worth; in 1933 we exported $7,600,000 worth. We had a gain of $2,000,000 to the United Kingdom but we lost $20,000,000 in exports of lumber to the United States. That is what happens in retaliation for our high duties. The same thing has happened in connection with imports. Duties have not been collected because goods have not been coming in. As I have said before, our hon. friends are creating a vicious circle. In the first place they are cutting off the market for our producers' goods; in the next place they are cutting off the revenue from customs duties because no goods are coming in in exchange
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

for those producers' goods; in the next place they are imposing a tax on the man who has lost his trade. These extra taxes have to be imposed to make up the loss.
One cent has been taken off the sugar tax. I should like to read the remarks made by the Prime Minister when the government of which I happened to be a humble member took off the tax on tea. He quoted Mr. Lloyd George's speech, and then in Hansard of 1930, page 1830, he said.:
I commend that to the government opposite: Go and tell the housewife that you are taking the duty off tea now; that last year you took the duty off cheques, parlour and sleeping car tickets; and that this year you are taking the duty off tea on the eve of an election. I cannot without having before me the figures express any opinion with respect to the condition of the revenue generally but I should say that if there is one war tax in all the *world that should have been dealt with as soon as possible it was the tax on tea. Every member of this house will say that. But, as a matter of fact, the government had not seen fit to take the tax off tea until now, on the eve of an election. Who will say, in the words of Lloyd George, that there was no bribery in that? Those were his words, not mine.
At the most there is only one year more before an election and so my hon. friends are getting ready to meet the housewife and say to her, "We have taken off one cent of the tax on your sugar bowl."
I should like to deal with the tax which has been placed on gold. My hon. friend is endeavouring to make up his revenue by imposing a tax which has created a good deal of alarm all over the Dominion of Canada and particularly in certain sections. Let me say to him that I do not think there is an industry in Canada ^rhich has attracted so much United States capital in the last two or three years as the gold mining industry. The Minister of Finance has said that he is anxious to attract United States and English capital. We are proud of this industry. It is one which has created a demand for skilled and unskilled employment; it has created a need for timber, steel, dynamite, chemicals, machinery and many other things in connection with its operations; it has created a need for fuel, food, clothing and other household supplies on the part of those employed in the mines. This industry has supplied a good deal of the freight and a good deal of the passengers carried by our railways. It has supplied an opportunity for development to the power companies and has been the cause of new hydro-electric enterprises being brought to completion. This industry has been one of the most important of any industry we have in the production of wealth. There is no need

of a sales agent to dispose of its product, as there is a ready market. There is no question of price, as the price is fixed. We in this country have been able to pay a good many bills and to buy many of the things we have bought from outside, such as cotton, rubber, fruits and manufactured goods, with the gold produced by our mines. These mines are taxed already. The mines themselves pay a corporation income tax while the shareholders pay the income tax which is imposed upon individuals. My hon. friend now proposes to impose a further tax because of the artificial increase which has occurred in the price of gold.
There is something in the argument which he puts forward. I do not suggest that the tax is wholly bad by any means but I am suggesting that there seems to be a lack of appreciation of the fact that there are other industries in this country which have been able artificially to increase their prices because of government action. These industries have not been placed in the same category with the gold mines. The consumer pays an increased price because of government interference with other industries of this country, but no extra tax is being imposed on them. Outside of the two major points which I shall mention in a moment, there are other features which give difficulty in connection with this tax. First, it is discrimination against a particular industry and, second, it is discrimination against particular sections of Canada. All parts of Canada do not get the benefit of gold mines. The little province which I have the honour to represent has done some gold mining but to a very limited extent. We hope to have further developments. There is gold mining done \n Quebec and there is a great deal in Ontario. Manitoba has some while British Columbia has a good deal. One or two of the western provinces have produced traces of gold, while we all know what has been done in the Yukon. Generally speaking, the bulk of this taxation will fall upon two or three sections of this dominion.
My hon. friend was in this position:	He
had put his duties up so high that he could not get any money. He did not want to continue the two-cent sugar tax, but where needs must, the devil drives. He had to get money from somewhere, and he said, "We will call on the gold industry." Had we been in the comer in which he is, we might have done exactly the same thing but I can assure him that we would not have done it in the same way. We would not have made the same proposal which he made in his budget

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
speech. In the first place, he taxes production and not profits. I say to him that he cannot possibly justify a tax which discriminates between a mine which can produce an ounce of gold from seven or eight tons of ore and another mine which can produce a similar quantity from only three tons. In the case of one mine it may cost $29 to produce *n ounce of gold while with another mine, it may cost $31. Regardless of this my hon. friend is proposing to tax everything received above $30 an ounce up to 10 per cent of the gross price received, I say that that is wrong and it cannot be justified. The low-grade mines will be paying a percentage beyond all reason when compared with other mines producing a higher grade ore.
Let me put an example on the record. Assume that it costs a mine $14 to procure an ounce of gold. They obtain $35 for that gold, giving a profit of $21. The tax will be ten per cent of that $35, or $3.50, which means sixteen per cent of the profit of $21. Another mine producing low grade ore finds that it costs $31 to produce an ounce of gold. That gold is sold for $35, giving a profit of $4. In this case the tax is the same, ten per cent on the $35, which leaves a profit of only fifty cents per ounce. The tax amounts to 87J per cent of the profit. Now can the Minister of Finance justify any such taxation as that? My hon. friend to my left has suggested that in the case of some mines this tax will mean bankruptcy and the closing down of operations. Assume that it costs a mine $32 to produce an ounce of gold; that mine would have a profit of only $3 per ounce while it would be taxed $3.50 per ounce on the gold it produces; it would have a loss of fifty cents on every ounce of gold it produced. That means bankruptcy. And what does that mean? It means that the mines which are giving the most employment, providing an opportunity for supplying the greatest amount of material, the mines which require the handling of the greatest amount of ore, and the mines that are least able to pay are taxed the most-taxed out of existence. It is absolutely unfair and inequitable and cannot possibly be justified.
Secondly, let me point this out-and I appeal to the Minister of Finance, because he and I come from the same province. The hon. gentleman knows that in our own province particularly the mines there are in process of development now, and the little gold that is being produced, while it is being realized upon, is not providing money to be used in profits. Dividends are not being paid but the money is being turned back into the mines
for purposes of development. I submit therefore that they should not be taxed, but they will be taxed under this provision, because 10 per cent of production is taken. My hon. friend ought to have special consideration for these mines. I believe that the tax in its present form is inequitable and indefensible, and will do incalculable injury to the dominion. It was none other than the Prime Minister himself who on March 27, 1033, as reported in Hansard, page 3424, with regard to the gold mining industry, made a statement which I think might very well be quoted on this occasion. He said:
This country at the present moment has reached a margin of borrowing which, under the ordinary rules that govern, according to the books, is almost its maximum borrowing power unless you have a rapidly increasing population or great natural resources that are being rapidly developed. That is the reason that the increase in gold production in this country has added relatively so greatly to confidence in the country. And the reason is obvious.	[DOT]
But my right hon. friend undermines confidence when he taxes the gold mining industry in this inequitable fashion and shuts down the very mines that would do most good in the development of this country. Let me refer to a statement made by the Minister of Mines (Mr. Gordon), a member of this government, at Quebec, at a meeting of the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy. This is what he said as reported in the Canadian Northern Miner of April 12, 1934:
"I should like to touch on the policy of the dominion government toward taxation of mining profits," the -minister said. "Some hold to the belief we should exact from the industry, particularly from the gold producing companies, a greater share of their profits. But which is the better course? To maintain stable taxation and thereby afford greater development of our gold resources with consequent greater return to the dominion's exchequer or to discourage this development by thinking up ways and means of deriving greater taxation from the industry? As I stated before foreign capital is in large measure supporting the ever-increasing number of prospectors and others investigating our gold possibilities.
It is obvious then any undue stricture placed upon the profits of gold mines would result in Canada, as it has in other countries, in the slowing up of the stream of speculative money needed for gold mining development."
That was what the Minister of Mines had to say, and I suggest that the mining men of this country had a right to take it from that statement that the minister, as a member of the government, was intimating that the industry would not be taxed as it is at the present moment. I am sure that they did draw that inference. It was an assurance from

The Budget

Mr. Ralston
the Minister of Mines which this government would do well to honour.
I wish now to say a word in regard to the provision respecting coal. I can only say that I have endeavoured to find out what effect the change in the regulations in connection with drawbacks will have, but I am afraid the matter will have to be left until we reach the committee stage when we can ascertain exactly how much coal is affected. I understand that the change made with respect to coal under item 1049 is that the drawback, which was previously 99 per cent of the duty, is now altered to 50 per cent, but that the incidence of the drawback, the benefits under it, will now be extended to gas retort plants as well as to by-product coke ovens. That means that you have an increased duty by 50 per cent and at the same time you may have an increase by 50 per cent in the number of those who are entitled to the benefit of the drawback. That will have to be left to the committee stage, when one can make intelligent observations on it. If it means that there is to be a further restriction with regard to competing American coal, then so far as I am concerned, coming as I do from Nova Scotia, I welcome it because if there is to be a policy of protection of natural products, the products of Nova Scotia as well as of other provinces should be protected, particularly in view of the national interests which exist in connection with the preservation of the mines of that province.
Let me now mention only generally the tariff as dealt with in the budget. I am not going into the items; I do not know enough about them, and we shall have an opportunity, in committee on ways and means, to discuss them. Generally speaking, I take it that they are pretty nearly what they appear to be, minor adjustments in the tariff. I am sorry that they do not seem to represent any decided change of heart, any rightabout face on the part of the government with respect to tariff matters. I find that peanut oil, beads, harps and cricket balls are all dealt with, and these articles would indicate the generally frivolous nature of most of the tariff items.
But what I do wish to refer to particularly is a matter which I regard as of much more importance than the individual items in the tariff, a matter of principle, and that is the appointment of the tariff board and the question of the decisions of that board, as well as the way in which this government should honour the findings of the body which it has appointed to deal with tariff matters.
I brought up in committee of supply the other evening the jute twine matter, and I

feel I ought to put the salient points on record in connection with the discussion of this whole subject. Two years ago we appointed a tariff board. The Prime Minister intimated that he wished to secure the best tariff board he could get, and he went afield to find the man best qualified for the position of chairman. I find in Hansard of 1933, page 4836, this statement made by the Prime Minister with regard to Mr. Justice Sedgewielc, the chairman of the board. The Prime Minister said:
When we have to go to the bench for the purpose of securing an appointment, we do not do so because they are judges as such, or because I happen to be a member of the legal profession, but because in the very nature of things we must endeavour to secure for the positions the best talent we can command, with the idea in mind that not only will Canadians be proud of the appointment, but that those from other lands who come before that tribunal will say: Here is a man who discharges his duty in a manner worthy of the great traditions that belong to those who sit in judgment upon matters affecting the interests of the country as a whole. ... If the committee were interested I could give the names of members of the profession who said: You must not take this man from us; he is the most brilliant and the best qualified of the judges we have had for years on our bench in the trial division and in connection with bankruptcy. . . . May I make just one or two other observations with respect to the matter? I knew that in time of stress and strain this house might not think this the most desirable thing to do; yet I say to my colleagues in this House of Commons that canvassing the situation in its entirety and looking over the field in every part of the dominion from the Atlantic to the Pacific I know not where I could secure an appointee who would so fuly measure up to my concep- ' tion of the ability required to perform the tasks imposed upon him under the statute as the gentleman who has been selected.
The Prime Minister was speaking there of the present chairman of the tariff board. In the debate-I have not the reference-the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Yeniot) asked the Prime Minister whether he did not think it would be better to have the customs board retain their jurisdiction in the matter of appeals rather than have the appeals go direct from the appraisers to the tariff board. The Prime Minister intimated in the debate that he considered this bill provided the preferable way, namely, that appeals should be made directly from the customs officials, appraisers, to the tariff board.
A case came up before the customs officials and it was this: jute twine was being imported from Great Britain. Jute twine had, with other articles, been subject under our tariff to the provision of section 43 of the Customs Act which permitted the Minister

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
of National Revenue to make an arbitrary valuation for duty purposes of goods coming in. In other words, jute twine was subject to what we call the dumping duty by reason of the fact that the minister was able to put an arbitrary valuation on the invoice. In November, 1932, we passed a statute amending our act and in view of the imperial conference agreements, we excepted from the provisions of section 43, goods coming in from Great Britain, so that after that date the minister was not permitted to make an order fixing a value for duty purposes or, in other words, he was not permitted to impose the dumping duty.
An order of jute twine came in; it was referred to the customs officials and notwithstanding the fact that the act had been amended in 1932, those officials held that the old order the minister had made still applied; they imposed a value for duty purposes on this particular shipment of jute twine and it was subjected to dumping duty. The matter was taken to the tariff board on appeal as was provided for at the time the legislation constituting the board was passed by this house. A decision was given; in fact, there were two decisions. The tariff board on October 30,
1933,	decided that the dumping duty did not apply to goods coming from the United Kingdom because the statute of 1932 expressly exempted British goods from that dumping duty. That decision was made by the tariff board and handed down on October 30, 1933. Did the government accept that decision? They did not. Did the Department of National Revenue accept the decision? They did not. Did they keep on imposing dumping duties? They did; notwithstanding the fact that their own board, headed by the gentleman who is mentioned by the Prime Minister in the passage I have just read, handed down a decision that they should not impose the dumping duty, they kept on doing so and not until after February 10, 1934, did the government accede even sufficiently to say: Well, while this matter is under discussion we will not insist on the dumping duty being paid. I have in my possession, not here, but in my office, a letter written by the Department of National Revenue on February 10,
1934,	telling the shipper that he has still to pay the dumping duty, notwithstanding the fact that the tariff board handed down their decision on October 30, 1933. That was not based on the ground that there was a serious question of law involved; I have been unable to find a single legal officer of any description who has given the opinion that the tariff board were wrong in their decision in that respect. Second, I have been unable to find anybody,
although I have asked the minister pretty persistently, who could suggest there was an appeal from the tariff board to the governor in council, although an appeal was at least pro forma taken in order to hold things up.

I would like my hon. friend to read the letter. I do not want to say anything unfair. It seems as if the letter meant what I thought it did.
As a matter of fact, that is the situation with regard to the decision of the tariff board and the government prior to February 10 declined to accept th t decision. Since then they have issued a circular in which they have intimated that while the matter is on appeal or at least referred to the Supreme Court of Canada, they will not impose the dumping duty, but that importers must be prepared to amend their entries should an adverse decision be handed down. Let me point this out: The appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada is not an appeal in connection with the matter which the tariff board decided. The board decided that the dumping duty could not be applied on a British shipment on account of the statute of November, 1932. What has gone to the Supreme Court of Canada? The reference to it is; did the tariff board have authority to decide that? They leave to one side entirely the question whether the tariff board were right in their decision; they are endeavouring only to test the authority. Does any importer care anything about the question of authority? Who ought to decide the question of the authority of the tariff board? It seems to me it is this parliament. Did we intend to give the tariff board authority to act in place of the customs board? If we did, we should say so by legislation and not by going to the Supreme Court of Canada.
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

Did the tariff board decide properly when they made their ruling?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The question is: Had the tariff board authority to decide? It was a very ingeniously put question. The question that should have been submitted to the Supreme Court was whether the tariff board were right or wrong in their decision, but the government have seen fit to submit not that question, but whether the tariff board have the right to make the decision, thus leaving entirely aside the merit of the decision itself in which, after all, not only are the importers interested but, I would think, the jute twine firms on the other side. Surely in connection with a matter of that kind my hon. friends opposite who are so anxious to promote the imperial conference agreements, would consider it a matter of honour that the provisions of those agreements which propounded that any dumping duty or exchange duty
fMr. Ralston.]
should be done away with as soon as possible should be carried out. Yet I find my hon. friends carrying this thing along, paying no attention to the tariff board decision, charging importers this dumping duty just the same as before and doing everything they can to be just as niggardly as possible in complying with the provisions of the imperial conference agreements, and, secondly, making all the trouble they can for the business people of this country. That, however, is not half as important or serious as that the government of this country should in the face of a decision made by a tribunal appointed by itself, treat it with absolute contempt, indeed, such contempt as could be punished as such if it were committed by an ordinary litigant before a court. They pay no attention to the decision, and thus hold the tariff board up to possible ridicule or at least to the reflections of people generally who say that evidently the board has not much standing; or at any rate the government does not pay any attention to it. I submit that the action of this government in connection with the tariff board in the jute twine case cannot be too strongly condemned by anyone who wants to see any stability in this country in connection with tariff matters.
The other case was the so-called "tin plate" case. Tin plate was being imported into this country. The Ojibway plant had said that they were closing down; in fact, they had closed down. The question was, whether tin plate which was being imported into this country by the canners, was after the Ojibway plant had closed down goods of a class or kind made in Canada. The customs people decided that it was, notwithstanding the fact that they had a letter there stating that the Ojibway plant was closed, and no other plant was operating here. Nevertheless the customs people decided that tin plate was a commodity of a class or kind made in Canada, because they said: There may be some on somebody's shelves, or it may be made some time, or perhaps it has been made. Therefore it imposed the 20 per cent duty and the dumping duty, instead of 15 per cent. That affected the fish canners, the fruit canners, and everybody in this country who used tin plate. The decision was handed down in that case in December, as far as I can remember, after the most strenuous efforts on the part of representatives of this government to keep that case dragging on before the tariff board. The first time they appeared and asked for one month's adjournment-I think that is right although I am not sure how long the first adjournment asked for was-but the second time the representatives of the government

The Budijet-Mr. Ralston
asked for a three months' adjournment. For what? In order that they might look into the question of the imperial conference agreements and find out whether tin plate was being manufactured in Canada. There was only one possible plant and that was at Sarnia where investigation could be made, and could be made promptly. The application was made for a three months'adjournment notwithstanding that in the meantime the importers in Canada would have to pay 20 per cent and the dumping duty. The tariff board did not grant three months' adjournment, but granted one month, and the board on December 12, made an order and said that tin plate was not a commodity of a class or kind made in Canada, and the dumping duty was not applicable. But it took two months before the customs issued an order with regard to that and decided that the tariff board decision had to be accepted at least for the period from June to December.
I cannot understand what the explanation is. But I say it does not speak well for the government, and it constitutes a reflection on the tariff board which they should not be under. It is injurious to the commercial interests of this country and contrary to the idea of the stability of tariff policy, because after all the Minister of Trade and Commerce in days gone by used to talk about the necessity for tariffs and import regulations being stable and being definite and certain. Apparently the government were trying to secure that by the appointment of this tariff board, but now when the}' get decisions they do not like they immediately disregard them. What sort of example is that to this country and to the other litigants appearing before the tariff board?
So I say, Mr. Speaker, that in the first place the government for nearly four months have refused to follow the decision of the tariff board with respect to the jute twine case. They have disregarded the decision of the tariff board of October 30, until very lately. Secondly, they have refused to follow the decision of the board in a similar case with regard to felt hats, which I have not mentioned. Thirdly, they have no opinion that an appeal lies from that decision. They have no opinion that the decision is not correct. Fourthly, in the tin plate case the government refused to accept and flouted the board's decision for two months at least. I say this is wrong because it wears out business people. It is not fair to the commercial community. It is wrong because it is not in keeping with the imperial conference agreements, and I say it is especially wrong because it discredits a 74726-1S5
board appointed by this government itself, and to which the people of Canada look for some stability in connection with tariff matters.
I have not dealt, Mr. Speaker, with all the matters which are contained in the budget but as I intimated to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, I hope I have demonstrated to him that at least there are some things about the budget of which I do not approve. After all I have said, Mr. Speaker, the most condemnatory criticism to be directed against this budget is that it shows that the government has neither the courage nor the capacity to follow through with their policy of trade restriction which was boasting]}' inaugurated at the special session of 1930. They have sown the wind and they are reaping the whirlwind. They find that Canada is not the only country which can restrict imports. They find, as a result, that Canada's former customers refuse to buy. They went into this trade war with the insane idea that they could give nothing and get everything by virtue of some heaven-sent superiority in commercial intelligence. The result is that the policy of strangling trade has increased costs of production to our farmers, fishermen, miners and lumbermen and, at the same time, the demand for their goods has been curtailed with a consequent drop in the prices of their products.
Having accomplished this tragedy in a country which depends so largely on exports of the farm, the forest, the mine, and the sea for its purchasing power, they-like Mark Twain who, in one of his stories, got his hero into such a fix that he said someone else would have to finish the book-now are forced to fall back on "the automatic working of fundamental economic forces," as they call it, to get them out.
Let there be no mistake, this country is now on the "dole" so far as export trade is concerned.
The problem is to bring about parity between the prices which the farmer and the other primary producers receive for their goods and the prices received for other commodities.
The Finance Minister, last year, deprecated economic nationalism. I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that economic nationalism for Canada began with the advent of the present government into power and they have constructed a "Frankenstein" which threatens to destroy them. At the special session of 1930 the Prime Minister held out shining hopes of the imperial conference which he was to attend in London. The net result was summed up in that descriptive comment "humbug". In

The Budget-Mr. Ralston

1932 my hon. friend the Prime Minister told us to look forward to the imperial economic conference at Ottawa for relief. Relief did not come. In 1933 he hoped that a world economic conference might save us. That conference is dead. They now supinely await for the working out of "present economic trends", surely a curious position for a party which was going to blast Canada into prosperity.
We must face the fact, Mr. Speaker, that the continuance of present policies has made it absolutely necessary to adopt no uncertain methods to bring about a parity between the price level of agricultural and other primary' products and the price level of other commodities and it is quite possible that the government of the day may be driven to drastic action in bringing about such a parity. A further consequence of continuing present policies might well be the necessity for the state to take the primary producer's surplus off his hands at a minimum price and market it abroad in a manner which will serve to increase, rather than to diminish, our total trade. This may be radical and this may appear to be artificial but it is a logical and almost inevitable consequence of a perpetuation of the economic nationalism to which this government has committed Canada.
I still believe, and those around me believe that it may not be too late, even yet, to extricate ourselves by paying attention to fundamentals. This country is in a different position from any other to promote export trade. There ought to be, and I still believe there could be an ordered and sensible readjustment of our fiscal policies, paying attention to the necessity for buying if we want to sell; at the same time giving our producers the purchasing power which comes from being able to dispose of their goods. Then we would have the home market for manufactured goods which has been talked about, but which has never been achieved by the present government. There need be no radical dislocation of business and industry, but there has to be a radical change in outlook and attitude, and whatever hope there may have been that this government would see the error of its ways, is shattered by the confession of helplessness contained in this budget. It is the climax of four years of inaction in which this country has been allowed to take the " shot and shell " of depression without the government attempting a single constructive operation, except counselling the troops to have courage and patience.
The Prime Minister repeatedly intimates that this and that can not be done. The trouble is that the budget is woefully lacking

in proposing anything which can be done, but the back and shoulders of Canada are near the breaking point under the strain of present conditions, and the great currents of business are dammed and stagnant by reason of the policies of this government. Armies on both our flanks have, by active, aggressive measures, succeeded in driving depression back, and just now the government, cautiously peeping over the parapet, suddenly discovers that the enemy is retiring and the Minister of Finance indicates to his apparent surprise that,
... it is now clear-that in several countries it began as early as the summer of 1932, and in the United Kingdom, even earlier.
And so they sit down on the fire step and complacently propose that we wait for the "automatic working of fundamental economic forces" and the effect of "present economic trends," which "are in the direction of further progress."
What is really needed is a persistent, determined, planned drive to clear the field. Can anyone question that Canada's success in that drive depends in no small degree on the development of her export trade? The Minister of Finance despondently tells us that:
International trade remains at a low level. Little, if any, progress has been made in removing the excessive interference with trade, the arbitrary quotas, the exchange controls and the other defensive measures which have been designed to meet the dangers of currency depreciation and unfavourable balances of payments.
I ask him what his government has done to undo the injury caused by its own policy of shackling Canada's trade by these very measures to which he refers. Admittedly, Mr. Speaker, we have gone so far that we cannot retrace our steps all at once, but it is because this budget does not give a sign of even halting, let alone turning right-about face and marching in the other direction, that I regard it as the most hopeless and discouraging budget speech which has been delivered during the four years of this parliament.
The reassuring aspect of the matter is that, judging by the results of five by-elections, climaxed by South Oxford, the country will, at the earliest opportunity, remove this government from power and register unmistakably its opinion that- its policies have proved a disastrous and costly failure for the people of this dominion. The people of Canada realize that the self-complacent, static attitude of mind reflected by this budget has already lost to Canada opportunities and prospects which will take her years to recover. They know

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
now that every day under the policies of the present government means so much lost ground which must be later regained, and they look forward eagerly to a general election to return a Liberal government to carry out-as Liberal governments have repeatedly done in the past -the task of recovery and reconstruction. And so I beg to move, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie), that all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
This house regrets that the proposals of the Minister of Finance give no indication of the intention of the government to abandon the policies of economic nationalism which have proved so disastrous to Canada's trade.
It is of the opinion that the immediate substitution therefor of policies which will promote ex-port trade throughout the world is essential to any permanent improvement of conditions in Canada, and to the successful application of other policies respecting credit and employment designed to effect this end.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) will not expect me, I am sure, to follow his very lengthy criticism. I must say that although it took a good deal of time for him to make his address I really do not find that I have any very concrete idea of exactly wherein his criticism lies, and I do not know that the amendment has clarified the situation very much. It is in such very general terms that one can make almost anything or nothing out of it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why don't you cross the floor?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Some hon. gentlemen here ask why I do not cross the floor. As a matter of fact some of us have been in this corner while two or three successive governments have crossed the floor.
The budget speech contains a general survey of financial conditions in Canada, and although it also covered a great deal of ground I think there are two or three outstanding points of which the general public ought to be made aware. First of all, and in my judgment very significant, is the increase in net debt during the year, on all accounts, of $135,200,000. I fancy the government is precisely in the position that any private business or individual is in; when you have to borrow money to pay interest on what you owe you are indeed in a bad way. It does not make much difference if the rate at which we are going into debt is a little less this year than it was last year; the fact is that this year's deficit is simply piled on top of last year's deficit.
We are also told that the reduction in controllable expenditures cannot go further. Looking to the future that does not give us a very great deal of hope. The reduction in controllable expenditures cannot go further, and I cannot but think of the hardship that has been caused by the reduction to date and the fact that very essential services have had to be curtailed or cut off entirely. On the other hand we are told that the increase in uncontrollable expenditures is bound to continue; that is, we have a debt which is expanding and on which the interest necessarily must increase also from year to year. So that is the unsatisfactory state of the country as a whole; we have controllable expenditures cut to the limit and uncontrollable expenditures bound to increase in the future.
I think one paragraph in the budget speech ought to be read into Hansard, because it summarizes the situation very well. It appears on page 2283 of Hansard:
In the year which has just closed, such expenditures-
This excludes the amounts required for the railway deficit and unemployment relief.
-totalled $364,000,000. Of this amount, $230,000,000 was required for purposes classed as uncontrollable and $134,000,000 for controllable. In other words, out of every $100 expended $03 went for expenses designated as uncontrollable and $37 for services that are ordinarly regarded as controllable. The main services under uncontrollable are interest on public debt amounting to $139,700,000; war pensions, $41,700,000 and treatment and aftercare of returned soldiers, $9,500,000.
These three items alone account for 83 per cent of the expenditure included' under the category of uncontrollable.
And perhaps it should be added that the cost of administering the public debt is not included in uncontrollable expenditures. The only comfort the Minister of Finance gives us is that the burden of our public debt is not beyond the capacity of our people to pay. That is, he joins with the Prime Minister in asking the common people to tighten their belts.
Now we come to the taxes imposed through which we are to meet the proposed expenditures. I am pleased to find that there is a reduction of one cent per pound on sugar. The stamp tax on postal notes issued in the amount of one dollar and under is reduced by one cent. I suppose small mercies should be thankfully received.

speechtext: A one cent budget.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It might very well be called a one cent budget. To make up for these very slight reductions on one or two

The Budget-Mr. TVoodsworth
items we have the tax on gold. Again, that we may have this clearly before us, I should like to read the paragraph dealing with this tax:
To replace, the revenue lost by the reduction in the tax on sugar, it is proposed to levy a tax of ten per cent on gold. In this connection one must keep in mind the fact that since our abandonment of the gold standard the price of gold in Canadian currency has risen from $20.67 an ounce to approximately $35. This is an increase in the selling price of the product of our gold mines of about 70 per cent. Furthermore, the extraordinary increase in the profits which accordingly accrue to gold producers find its origin in circumstances entirely external to this particular industry. That is to say, the reason for this increase in price is to be found in the chaotic conditions of world currencies, the depreciation of our dollar in the foreign exchanges and the devaluation of gold by certain countries.
These gains to the gold miners are classed as "fortuitous gains." I commend the Minister of Finance for so clearly pointing that out-fortuitous gains. One of the least satisfactory portions of the speech to which we have just listened is that dealing with the proposed tax on gold.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does that apply to all
the gold mines?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The financial critic of the opposition has suggested that this tax means a discrimination against a particular industry. Well, I would point out that that is true of all our indirect taxation. Our whole tariff schedule means that particular industries are singled out for taxation, so there is nothing new in that contention. Further than that, it is suggested that it is discrimination against particular parts of the country. That, too, is true under our present system of taxation. Wheat is grown in one part of the country and furniture is manufactured in another part. Undoubtedly it might be said that any indirect taxation of that kind is a discrimination against some particular section of the country. Further it is suggested that the budget does not take into account the variations in the grades of ore and costs of production. I do not believe it is common that such variation should be taken into account. If we did fully take -them into account it would be a bonusing [DOT]of the marginal mines. Since this enormous -gain in the value of gold is entirely a fortuitous gain-and I think that cannot be gainsaid-my question is: Why take only ten per cent? Why not take the entire fortuitous gain? I can see no reason why that should not be done. Gold is in a different position from any other commodity, since owing to

governmental action it has become the measure of all other commodities. It is in an unique position. And if owing very largely to governmental action we have turned over millions upon millions of dollars to the people who at the present time have control of gold mines, and that action has meant to them an increase from $20.67 an ounce to $35, there seems no reason why the public should not gain the advantage of such increase. Of course, some one will say that would mean that certain mines would not be able to gain as much as they are doing to-day, that certain lower grade mines would be discriminated against, that a certain number of men would be turned out of work, and so on. I know there may be all these objections, but they apply equally in any taxation of this kind, because a good many industries have been put out of business through the very high taxation placed upon them in the purchase of the raw materials required for their products. Personally I think that if gold is as necessary in the carrying on of our trade as everyone seems to imagine, the only permanent solution would be for the government to take over the gold mines. They could then keep the miners at work on a reasonable wage scale; they would then be able to collect this fortuitous gain instead of turning it over to private individuals.
I note that therfe is no change whatever in the income tax. I am glad that it has not been lessened, but it does seem to me that the income tax ought to be a source of much greater revenue than it is at the present time. There is no reason why it should not be more steeply graded. Only a few days ago I noticed a very interesting editorial in the Gazette of March 19 headed, "On the Income Tax," and based on an article in the National Revenue Review. Since this editorial appears in such a highly respected journal, I believe I may read a paragraph or so:
Whilst the Canadian considers his income is too heavily taxed, he may find it intriguing, if not consoling, to compare his payments under this heading with the income tax the citizen of Great Britain pays. In Canada a single person in receipt of an income of $2,000 a year is liable for $30 income tax. A married man receiving a like income is exempt from payment. Single persons whose annual incomes are $5,000 pay $180 income tax and married persons $120. The scale continues as follows:
And then follows a table which I shall not give in detail. It will be noticed however that in case of higher grade incomes the British people are able to collect almost twice as much as we collect from similar grades in Canada, I would suggest that those people

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
who are so very anxious to copy British institutions might very well copy some of the British policies with regard to income and inheritance tax.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? In making his last observation has he borne in mind the circumstance that the British people pay only one income tax, while in Canada in many instances we have three?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I recognize that fact, but I do not believe it alters the situation in the slightest. It might mean that the man who pays an income tax would have to pay a little bit more, but the principle is that great wealth ought to carry a very large proportion of the load. That is not being done either in our provincial or federal spheres. That is, the grading is not nearly as steep in this country as it is in Great Britain. With regard to taxation I should like to give to the house the plank in our C.C.F. platform outlining our policy in that connection. It is as follows:
11. Taxation and' public finance!
A new taxation policy designed not only to raise public revenues but also to lessen the glaring inequalities of income and to provide funds for social services and the socialization of industry; the cessation of the debtcreating system of public finance.	[DOT]
The explanatory note reads:
In the type of economy that we envisage the need for taxation, as we now understand it, will have largely disappeared. It will nevertheless be essential, during the transition period, to use the taxing powers, along with the other methods proposed elsewhere, as a means of providing for the socialization of industry, and for extending the benefits of increased social services.
At the present time capitalist governments in Canada raise a large proportion of their revenues from such levies as customs duties and sales taxes, the main portion of which falls upon the masses. In place of such taxes upon articles of general consumption, we propose the drastic extension of income, corporation and inheritance taxes, steeply graduated according to ability to pay. Full publicity must be given to income tax payments and our tax collection system must be brought up to the English standard of efficiency.	.
We also believe in the necessity for an immediate revision of the basis of dominion and provincial sources of revenue, so as to produce a coordinated and equitable system of taxation throughout Canada.
An inevitable defect of the capitalist system is the debtcreating character of public finances. All public debts have enormously increased and the fixed interest charges paid thereon now amount to the largest single item of so-called uncontrollable public expenditures. The C.C.F. proposes that in future no public financing shall be permitted which facilitates the perpetuation of the parasitic interestreceiving
class; that capital shall be provided through the medium of the national investment board and free from perpetual interest charges.
We propose that all public works, as directed by the planning commission, shall be financed by the issuance of credit as suggested, based upon the national wealth of Canada.
I should like to take this opportunity to suggest that there are certain economies which are not dealt with by the Minister of Finance and which I think should be considered by the country as a whole. Having in mind the general Canadian situation, I think first of the possibility of combining some of our provincial administrations. I can see no reason why the expensive arrangement under which we have three maritime provinces and three prairie provinces should be continued. It would seem to me that we might very well combine the maritimes and the prairie provinces, and thus cut down part of the load which is being carried by the people of this country.
As another example I would call attention to the enormous expenditures in connection with the administration of justice. The number of judges in this country is out of all proportion to the population. I cannot see why the speech of the Minister of Finance should not be made the occasion for considering some of these extravagances in the administration of our affairs. There are certain ways in which we could promote efficiency and at the same time cut down expenditure. Why should not our estimates be considered in appropriate committees? The government will have to undertake to initiate such reforms. I am glad to note that the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has suggested that the time is coming when there should be a revision of the British North America Act under which there might be a redistribution of the powers as between the dominion and the provinces. Here again I wonder if I might be permitted to read the proposals of the C.C.F. in this matter. They are:
9. B.N.A. Act:
The amendment of the Canadian constitution, without infringing upon racial or religious minority rights or upon legitimate provincial claims to autonomy, so as to give the dominion government adequate powers to deal effectively with urgent economic problems which are essentially national in scope; the abolition of the Canadian Senate.
Then the explanatory note is as follows:
We propose that the necessary amendments to the British North America Act shall be obtained as speedily as required, safeguards being inserted to ensure that the existing rights of racial and religious minorities shall not be changed without their own consent. What is chiefly needed to-day is the placing in the hands of the national government of more power to

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
control national economic development. In a rapidly changing economic environment our political constitution must be reasonably flexible.^ The present division of powers between dominion and provinces reflects the conditions of a pioneer, mainly agricultural, community in 1867. Our constitution must be brought into line with the increasing industrialization of the country and the consequent centralization of economic and financial power which has taken place in the last two generations. The principle laid down in the Quebec resolutions of the Fathers of Confederation, should be applied to the conditions of 1933, that "there be a general government charged with matters of common interest to the whole country and local governments for each of the provinces charged with the control of local matters in their respective sections."
The Canadian Senate, which was originally created to protect provincial rights, but has failed even in this function, has developed into a bulwark of capitalist interest, as is indicated by the large number of company directorships held by its aged members. In its peculiar composition of a fixed number of members appointed for life, it is one of the most reactionary assemblies in the civilized world. It is a standing obstacle to all progressive legislation, and the only permanently satisfactory method of dealing with the constitutional difficulties it creates is to abolish it.
It does seem to me that if the government would make a thorough survey of the situation which exists to-day in Canada, it might reduce considerably the enormous burden which, according to this budget speech, will continue to be borne by the people.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In this budget, as in most recent budgets, a very considerable proportion of the expenditure is on what is known as uncontrollable expenditures. May I point out that these expenditures are not really uncontrollable; they are uncontrollable only in so far as the government in power is determined to maintain the status quo. The financial critic of the government, who preceded me, called attention to the possibility of converting our national debts. We ought to have impressed upon this house the remarks made by the Prime Minister himself before the committee on monetary, and financial questions at the imperial conference of 1932. I quoted them in my speech on the address, but I think they cannot be too clearly put before the public. The right hon. gentleman said:
Interest charges represent the most important of the fixed or semi-rigid elements in our cost structure. If prices remain on their present

level, such charges will constitute an intolerable or almost intolerable burden in many cases. Even if it can be borne, the fortuitous gain-
May I direct attention to that phrase, which is also used in the budget speech this year. -the fortuitous gain to the creditor of 40 to 48 per cent in general purchasing power above what he contracted for appears to be a grave injustice.
The Prime Minister clearly recognized the injustice of permitting bondholders and others who hold mortgages in this country to receive from 40 to 48 per cent more than they should, but he has done nothing about it. This budget continues that arrangement, and all we are told is that these expenditures are uncontrollable. To continue:
One of the most important effects of the fall in prices is the increased burden of the fixed charges payable on our governmental and private obligations held abroad, chiefly in the United States and the United Kingdom. ... As one dollar to-day will purchase at wholesale 48 per cent more than it did in 1929, the real burden of the service charges on these foreign obligations has increased from $362,000,000 to $535,750,000.
These expenditures are said to be uncontrollable, but there seems to be no reason whatever why we should not deal with our debts, cutting them down at least to the point where they have the same buying power as they had when the debts were contracted. The Prime Minister admits that this would be fair but nothing is done about it. It is suggested by the Minister of Finance that we could not contemplate cutting down the debts, making any change in the bonds held by people outside Canada. I understand however that the great proportion of the bonds are held by people inside Canada, and they at any rate can be dealt with; and as regards those held outside, I might point out that a great many nations including Great Britain have in effect cut down their debts in this way.
The Prime Minister told us the other day that in raising the resources he is not actuated by party considerations. That may be true, but I think that the budget clearly demonstrates that he is actuated by class considerations, because from beginning to end the taxes rest most heavily proportionately upon the poor and least heavily upon the very wealthy; and I think it is fair to say of this budget, as of several preceding budgets, that the effect is to make the rich richer and the poor poorer. We believe that the taxation policy should be used to lessen at least in some degree the glaring inequalities of income. On the contrary, the taxing powers are here being used to increase that glaring injustice and to make

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
life still more intolerable for the poor, while the poor man passes over through interest charges a very considerable amount of his earnings to those who are already rich.
The Prime Minister the other day defended tax-exempt bonds on the ground that they represent absolute stability and security. I should like to ask him-What about the stability and security of the masses of the people? They have nothing of that stability and security to-day. The great majority of our business men do not know what to do in order to carry their small overhead; they do not know what day they will be faced with bankruptcy; and as for the labour men, they are not secure even in the opportunity of making a living.
It is very delightful indeed to witness a godfather presenting a child with a thousand dollar bond. The Prime Minister would not like in any way to deprive us of the pleasure of enjoying that very pretty picture, but I submit that there are a great many people to-day who are losing their homes and farms. I fancy nearly all of us have received the most pathetic letters from friends throughout the west where at most a few hundred dollars would save them their homes. But they have not that money and so they are losing their farms, essentially, as my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) says, in order that we may pay these interest charges and thus maintain the stability and security of certain classes.
The Prime Minister the other day pointed out the danger of impairing the resources of estates in trust, all those estates that were used in caring for the sick, the afflicted or for scientific research. But I would point out that there are a great many sick not provided for in this land. And what about even the children in our public schools who have not an opportunity of carrying forward their education, some of them not having even the chance of an ordinary decent life. In this connection I would read two or three paragraphs from an article in a recent number of The Canadian Forum on economic conditions in rural Saskatchewan by G. E. Britnell. He is summarizing and interpreting the final bulletin No. 19 of the seventh census of Canada. He says that 5,036 out of the 288,0C0 farms of the prairie provinces have water piped in the kitchen; or, reduced to more manageable proportions, that only one out of every 57-2 farms in western Canada enjoys this convenience, while in Ontario the corresponding ratio is one out of every 9-54. He points out that in
the west one out of every 72-8 has water piped in the bathroom-it would be interesting to know how many have a bathroom of any kind-as compared with one out of 15-76 in Ontario. One out of every 34-44 western farm homes is lighted by gas or electricity as compared with one out of 5-95 in Ontario. That shows the entire lack of what in the cities would be regarded as absolute necessities. The article continues:
The average farm home in Saskatchewan showed few signs of extravagance in the small cheaply-built frame house, the inexpensive but uncomfortably primitive heating system, the coal-oil and gasoline lamps, the cheap and inadequate furniture and the almost total lack of domestic conveniences.
And still further:
Fresh fruit was the greatest possible luxury while farm children seldom saw oranges from one Christmas to another. Over wide areas of the province medical facilities were inadequate; after the prairie trails had disappeared, the roads, when once the traveller left the few half-graded dirt highways, must have been among the worst in the world; the cultural life of the farm community tended to continue as barren as that characteristic of all agrarian frontiers.
And again:
Official figures illustrate graphically the extent of the financial collapse. For instance, it is reported "that forty rural municipalities, fifty villages and twenty-seven towns have defaulted in their debenture payments. In addition S28 rural school districts, 225 village school districts and forty-eight town school districts have defaulted in the payment of their debentures. ..." The bank indebtedness of rural municipalities at the end of 1932 was $8,379,548.97; the amount due schools, et cetera, for the requisition of taxes amounted to $8,120,615.71; the uncollected arrears of taxes plus the tax sale holdings (which must be added to get a correct statement of total arrears) amounted to $30,368,345.82.
And so forth. The article goes on to tell of the hardships of the farmers and of the very serious conditions which exist at the present time. My point is simply this: that whilst we talk grandly of maintaining the credit of the country, these deplorable conditions prevail in certain sections. Why is it so important to continue to pay not only one hundred cents but well on to one hundred and fifty cents on the dollar in real purchasing power to maintain those who hold bonds and to take it out of the pockets of people who have to live in conditions such as I have described?
The other day when I looked over this budget it reminded me somewhat of that old biblical story where the taskmasters of Egypt
The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth

required the people of Israel, who were practically their slaves, to make bricks without straw:
And the taskmakers hasted them saying, fulfil your works, your daily tasks, as when there was straw.
To all protests Pharaoh replied:
There shall no straw be given you, yet shall ye deliver the tale of bricks.
I might say that our modern Pharaoh insists on double the tale, as I have just explained. In fact, sometimes in this pressure that is being exerted, this tightening of the belt policy, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and his cabinet are something like Rehoboam of the old days who, following the counsel of the young men, declared:
My father made your yoke heavy, and I will add to your yoke.
Tighten your belts. The answer of the people was:
To your tents, 0 Israel.
I may win some applause from my friends the Liberals when I remind them that the people rejected Rehoboam as their king.
The Prime Minister has a curious mentality and I refer to him because it seems to me that this budget incorporates some of the principles he has been giving us from time to time in the house. The other day, speaking in connection with titles, he said:
God has not given equal ability to all men and women. They are not all equipped with the same power of thought or with the same intellectual power.
Therefore it would seem, if I read aright his deductions, that some ought to be given titles and greater wealth, greater privileges of all kinds than others. I wish I could impress upon the government and the Prime Minister the fact that wealth to-day comes very largely through the possession of special privileges. Some few people have got charters and leases and all that kind of thing and in that way the owners of those special privileges have made their money. Withdraw the special privileges and they would be in the same boat as the rest of us.
The other day I was reading an article showing the gradual extension of powers which all governments are now being forced to take to themselves, and how the assumption of new responsibilities meant reorganization. The article to which I refer is called Politics versus Economics and I especially ask my Liberal friends to read it. It is by Gustav Stolper in Foreign Affairs for April, 1934, and reads:
FMr. Woodsworth.]
But once the state comes into possession of the decisive instruments of power in capitalistic economy-money and credit'-it at once finds itself becoming responsible for prosperity and depression.
And again:
Budget policy, tax policy, credit policy, currency policy-all go to make up one indivisible unit. Anything done in any one of those departments has its effect on all the others. As master of taxation, the state is in direct control of a large portion of the national income; as master of railroad and public utility rates the state is in direct control of another large portion of the national income; as master of the credit markets the state has indirect command over investments; this state therefore cannot avoid taking currency under its control.
The article was referring particularly to the necessity of the state taking currency under its control and that, I am glad to say, is being done more or less under the bill introduced in regard to the Bank of Canada Act, although under that legislation currency still remains under private control. I should like to emphasize that we can no longer judge a budget by the same standards as we judged budgets some years ago. The government itself is having to assume very much greater responsibilities for the affairs of the nation and we have a right to expect that the government will be very largely responsible for initiating those policies which will lead to prosperity. The trouble, as I see it, is that the present government has not done anything that would fundamentally alter the existing economic system.
May I close by quoting a passage from an excellent elucidation of the findings of the Bureau of Economic Research. This is contained in the letter of the National City Bank of New York of April, 1934. Mr. Walter Lippmann summarizes the findings in this way, and I think it very well summarizes the budget as well:
From 1929 to 1932 there was a great decline in the total national income. But in the course of this decline salaries and dividend payments fell slowly at first. Interest payments fell very little. Among labour incomes salaried men were favoured as against wage earners, and of course wage earners as against the unemployed. Relatively speaking, property incomes increased. . . .
The figures show that the depression was not like some great accident, say a shipwreck, in which all suffered alike. They show, on the contrary, that the sacrifices were very uneven, and that worst of all, though nearly everybody was poorer, the distribution of wealth became progressively more and more unequal, taking the greatest toll from those who already were the weakest, and far greater toll from the active producers of wealth than from the recipients of fixed or sheltered incomes.

The Budget-Mr. Gobeil
Could any words better describe this budget? It takes the greatest toll from those who already were the weakest, and far greater toll from the active producers of wealth than from the recipients of fixed or sheltered incomes.
